name: Mark
author: The Gospel itself never names its writer, but from the early second century Christians credited it to Mark, traditionally identified with John Mark, a Jewish believer from Jerusalem whose mother's house was a meeting place for the first church. He travelled with his cousin Barnabas and with Paul, and later worked alongside Peter, and an early church leader named Papias said Mark wrote down Peter's memories of Jesus. Many scholars accept this tradition, while others think the author was an unknown Christian teacher. Most agree it was probably the first of the four Gospels to be written.
audience: Early tradition says Mark wrote for Christians in Rome, many of them not Jewish, which fits the way he explains Jewish customs and translates Aramaic words, the everyday language Jesus spoke. These believers may have been living through, or just after, the fierce persecution under Emperor Nero around AD 64, when Peter is said to have died. Some scholars instead suggest a church in Syria or Galilee.
era: Mark was probably written around AD 65–70, a frightening time when Jews in Judea rose up against Rome and the Roman army crushed the revolt, destroying Jerusalem's temple in AD 70. The events it describes took place about forty years earlier, around AD 30, in Galilee and Judea under Roman rule. Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, governed Galilee, while the Roman governor Pontius Pilate ruled Judea.

notes.1:21: Capernaum, a fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, became Jesus' base; a synagogue was the local Jewish meeting place for prayer and Scripture reading.
notes.2:13: Tax collectors gathered tolls for Herod Antipas and Rome, often taking extra for themselves, so fellow Jews widely despised them as cheats and collaborators.
notes.2:23: The Sabbath, from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset, was the weekly day of rest; Pharisees, a respected group devoted to strict law-keeping, counted plucking grain as forbidden harvesting work.
notes.3:1: The Herodians were supporters of Herod Antipas and his family, normally unlikely allies for the Pharisees.
notes.5:1: This took place on the lake's eastern side, near the Decapolis, a region of Greek-style cities where most people were not Jewish, which explains the herd of pigs.
notes.6:14: This 'King Herod' was Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee; the Jewish historian Josephus also records that he imprisoned and executed John the Baptist, at his fortress of Machaerus.
notes.7:24: Tyre was an ancient non-Jewish port city on the Mediterranean coast north of Galilee, in what is now Lebanon.
notes.8:27: Caesarea Philippi lay far north near Mount Hermon, a city rebuilt by Herod's son Philip, named after the emperor, and home to a shrine to the Greek god Pan.
notes.9:2: The mountain is not named; tradition identifies it as Mount Tabor in Galilee, though some suggest Mount Hermon near Caesarea Philippi.
notes.10:1: The region across the Jordan, called Perea, was also ruled by Herod Antipas, and divorce was a hotly debated question among Jewish teachers of the day.
notes.10:46: Jericho was the last town on the steep road up to Jerusalem, about fifteen miles away, and crowds of pilgrims passed through on their way to Passover.
notes.11:1: Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem, where the city was filling with pilgrims for Passover.
notes.11:15: In the temple's large outer court, traders sold animals for sacrifice and money changers swapped Roman coins for the special coinage required for the temple tax.
notes.12:13: The tax was a Roman tribute paid in silver denarius coins stamped with the emperor Tiberius' image, a sore point for many Jews.
notes.12:18: The Sadducees were a wealthy priestly group who rejected the Pharisees' unwritten traditions and did not believe in resurrection; some ancient writers say they accepted only the first five books of Scripture, though many scholars doubt this.
notes.12:41: The temple treasury probably refers to offering chests, said to be shaped like trumpets, that stood in the temple's Court of the Women.
notes.13:1: Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple around 20 BC with enormous white stones, and work was still continuing in Jesus' day.
notes.14:1: Passover, followed by the week-long Feast of Unleavened Bread, recalled Israel's escape from Egypt and drew huge crowds to Jerusalem each spring.
notes.14:12: Passover lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon before the Passover meal, and the meal had to be eaten within Jerusalem after sunset.
notes.14:32: Gethsemane, meaning 'oil press', was an olive grove on the slope of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley from the city.
notes.14:43: Later in this passage a young man runs away. Some have long suggested he was Mark himself, though the Gospel never says so.
notes.14:53: The council, often called the Sanhedrin, was the Jewish ruling body led by the high priest, who at this time was Caiaphas.
notes.15:1: Pontius Pilate, Roman governor of Judea from about AD 26 to 36, usually lived on the coast but came to Jerusalem at Passover to keep order.
notes.15:21: Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community; crucifixion was a public Roman execution reserved for rebels, slaves and serious criminals.
notes.16:9: The oldest surviving manuscripts end at verse 8; most scholars think these closing verses were added later, though some defend them and the church has long read them.
